abstracts.title: Non-PML neuroinvasive infections reported with multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapies: a mechanism-based pharmacovigilance study, 2004-2025.
abstracts.abstract: Background Multiple sclerosis (MS) disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) alter host immunity and may produce pathogen-specific susceptibility to neuroinvasive infection. Comparative evidence is limited because events are rare and postmarketing research focuses mainly on progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Methods We analyzed deduplicated US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) reports from 2004Q1 to 2025Q4 using a prespecified case-non-case design. Tier A comprised direct high-certainty non-PML neuroinvasive infection terms. Tier B comprised a possible CNS infectious syndrome plus pathogen evidence elsewhere in the report, without CNS confirmation; tier A+B was a lower-certainty expanded endpoint for sensitivity and pathogen composition analyses. We estimated overall reporting (E1), pathogen composition within tier A+B (E2), and same-pathogen CNS localization (E3). Five DMT mechanisms were compared with contemporaneous active DMTs using calendar-year Mantel-Haenszel reporting odds ratios and covariate-adjusted Jeffreys-prior penalized logistic models. Results Among 492,514 reports, 675 were tier A and 82 additional reports were tier B. Tier A aRORs (95% CIs) were…

abstracts.title: Is it time for anti-CD20 discontinuation in multiple sclerosis? Cumulative risk or cumulative uncertainty.
abstracts.abstract: The widespread adoption of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies (anti-CD20 mAbs) in multiple sclerosis (MS) has prompted increasing interest in treatment discontinuation and de-escalation strategies. In this perspective, we critically examine current data on outcomes following anti-CD20 discontinuation, including evidence from registries, prospective cohorts, and real-world studies. Available findings suggest that disease control achieved under anti-CD20 therapy is pharmacologically maintained rather than biologically resolved, and that B-cell repopulation following treatment cessation is heterogeneous and not reliably predictive of clinical stability. Reports of disease reactivation after discontinuation and the absence of validated biomarkers to identify patients who may safely stop therapy highlight substantial uncertainty. Current evidence therefore remains insufficient to support routine anti-CD20 discontinuation in MS, while a cautious, individualized approach-potentially incorporating dose-spacing strategies-may better reflect the current state of knowledge.

abstracts.title: Treatment Exit in Aging Multiple Sclerosis: A Critical Review of Discontinuation, De-Escalation, and Dose Reduction, with Implications for GCC Practice
abstracts.abstract: Background: Aging and prolonged disease stability prompt reassessment of multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapy. Discontinuation, switching, dose reduction and interval extension are distinct strategies. Stability during treatment may reflect reduced inflammatory activity, continuing drug effects, or both; chronological age alone cannot establish that withdrawal will preserve control. Objective: To critically assess treatment-exit evidence, reconcile apparently conflicting findings, distinguish treatment effects from prognostic associations, and examine implications for Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) practice. Approach: A targeted, web-assisted critical narrative review examined accessible primary studies, corrections, conference reports, trial registrations and regional documents through 1 November 2026. Comparisons considered population, mechanism, strategy, outcome, surveillance, residual exposure, restart and alignment of follow-up. No meta-analysis, independent duplicate screening or formal certainty grading was performed. abstracts.title: Risk of Inflammatory Bowel Disease After Anti-CD20 Treatment in Multiple Sclerosis.
abstracts.abstract: Importance Anti-CD20 biologics are widely used as disease-modifying therapy (DMT) for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), but recent reports have raised concerns about an increased risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) during treatment. This study aimed to assess treatment-associated IBD risk in individuals with RRMS. Objective To compare the risk of new-onset IBD across different therapies for RRMS and relative to the general population. Design, setting, and participants This was a population-based cohort study conducted in Sweden. Through the Swedish MS register, initiations of rituximab, natalizumab, dimethyl fumarate, and fingolimod were identified between January 1, 2011, and December 31, 2023, in individuals with RRMS aged 18 to 55 years with at least 10 years of lookback time (5 years for dispensed drugs) and no evidence of previous IBD. These initiations were matched with general population comparator episodes selected from the Swedish population. Exposures Rituximab, comparator DMTs (natalizumab, dimethyl fumarate, fingolimod), or general population comparator. abstracts.title: Diet quality, gut microbiome diversity, and clinical disability in multiple sclerosis: A cross-sectional case-control study.
abstracts.abstract: Dietary patterns and gut microbiome composition are increasingly recognised as modifiable factors in multiple sclerosis (MS). We aimed to evaluate dietary quality, microbiome diversity, and their inter-relationships with MS status, clinical disability, and disease-modifying therapy (DMT). We compared 288 MS cases with 274 household healthy controls (HHC). Dietary intake was assessed using healthy eating index (HEI-2015), and the groups were compared and associations analysed using multivariable linear regression. Among all HEI-2015 components, only total fruit intake was significantly higher in MS (β=+0.46; 95% CI: +0.19 to +0.74; FDR q = 0.014). Higher HEI-2015 scores were positively associated with greater Shannon alpha diversity (β=+0.077/10-unit increment; 95% CI: +0.003 to +0.150; p = 0.042). The PERMANOVA revealed independent association between microbiome beta diversity and smoking (R²=0.011; p = 0.007), BMI (R²=0.007; p = 0.010), age (R²=0.006; p = 0.027), and MS status (R²=0.005; p = 0.026), but not with diet quality (R²=0.006; p = 0.171). data.warnings_and_cautions: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Infusion Reactions: Management recommendations for infusion reactions depend on the type and severity of the reaction. Permanently discontinue OCREVUS if a life-threatening or disabling infusion reaction occurs ( 2.3 , 5.1 ) Infections: Serious, including life-threatening and fatal infections, have occurred. Delay OCREVUS administration in patients with an active infection until the infection is resolved. Vaccination with live-attenuated or live vaccines is not recommended during treatment with OCREVUS and after discontinuation, until B-cell repletion ( 5.2 ) Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML): Withhold OCREVUS at the first sign or symptom suggestive of PML ( 5.3 ) Reduction in Immunoglobulins: Monitor the level of immunoglobulins at the beginning of treatment. Monitor during and after discontinuation of treatment with OCREVUS, until B-cell repletion, and especially when recurrent serious infections are suspected. Consider discontinuing OCREVUS in patients with serious opportunistic or recurrent serious infections, and if prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia requires treatment with intravenous immunoglobulins ( 2.1 , 5.4 ) Malignancies: An increased risk of malignancy, including breast cancer, may exist with OCREVUS ( 5.5 ) Immune-Mediated Colitis: Immune-mediated colitis has been reported in the postmarketing setting. Monitor patients for new or persistent diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms, and evaluate promptly if colitis is su…

data.warnings_and_cautions: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Infections: Serious, including life-threatening and fatal infections, have occurred in patients treated with anti-CD20 therapies. Delay KESIMPTA administration in patients with an active infection until the infection is resolved. Vaccination with live-attenuated or live vaccines is not recommended during treatment with KESIMPTA and after discontinuation, until B-cell repletion. ( 5.1 ) Injection-Related Reactions and Hypersensitivity Reactions: Management for injection-related reactions and hypersensitivity reactions depends on the type and severity of the reaction. ( 4 , 5.2 ) Reduction in Immunoglobulins: Monitor the level of immunoglobulins at the beginning, during, and after discontinuation of treatment with KESIMPTA until B-cell repletion. Consider discontinuing KESIMPTA if a patient develops a serious opportunistic infection or recurrent infections if immunoglobulin levels indicate immune compromise. ( 5.3 ) Liver Injury: Clinically significant liver injury has occurred. Obtain serum aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin levels before initiating KESIMPTA, and during treatment as clinically indicated. Discontinue KESIMPTA in patients with evidence of liver injury in the absence of an alternative etiology. ( 5.4 ) Fetal Risk: May cause fetal harm based on animal data. Advise females of reproductive potential of the potential risk to a fetus and to use an effective method of contraception during treatment and for 6 months after…

Three approved drugs: ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, ublituximab. Multiple stopped trials: business reasons, slow enrollment, funding loss. RISK:cd20:MS shows median stop-risk 0.249. Literature highlights discontinuation uncertainty (PMID:42991313), IBD risk (PMID:42911175), and neuroinfection signals (PMID:42947820). ChEMBL failed. FDA labels confirm indications and warnings for ocrelizumab and ofatumumab. Competitors not directly named but implied in comparative studies.
